job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Gareth Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I get up at seven, bus to the building society's back office in Bristol, and spend the day matching supplier invoices to payments in a spreadsheet. I did accounting at a middling university, passed, no internships, and started here five months ago. I share a flat with two mates from school. My dad drives a bus and is his union's rep, so I grew up hearing about shifts and contracts at dinner. Evenings it's football, or my sister's kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, it's all marketing. The software at work has been about to change everything since I was at uni, and I still match invoices by hand every morning. Down the pub I'd say the bosses talk it up to justify cutting corners.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I don't use any of it and I'm fine with that. A small worry is that if the other juniors do, I look slow. But I got through a degree without it, so I think I'll cope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. I'd keep doing my invoices in the spreadsheet, keep paying my 520 a month for the room, and put 200 into savings like I do now. Maybe I'd finally go to the union branch meeting my dad keeps nagging me about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved, mostly. A bit bored too, because the job is repetitive and no hype is going to fix that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Setting AI aside, what about the next two years do you actually lose sleep over, if anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What bothers me is doing the same dull task for forty years, and the rent going up if our landlord sells. The nine thousand in my account takes the edge off, and my parents would help if it came to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If money got tight or work got harder anyway, who or what would you point to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd blame landlords and bosses who keep wages flat while profits go up. It's not the technology, it's who owns it.

say: I'd say the **hype** is mostly marketing to justify cutting corners.
I'd tell my mates the invoice software has promised big change for years and still needs me.
think: I'm quietly glad I **don't use** AI, though I fear looking slow next to other juniors.
My job and savings feel safe, so my real worry is **boredom**.
do: Keep matching invoices by hand and paying **520 a month** for my room.
Save **200 a month** as now, and finally attend a union branch meeting.
feel: **Relieved** that little changes, and a bit bored.
S0.quote: The software at work has been about to change everything since I was at uni, and I still match invoices by hand every morning.
fieldNote: **Settled** and secure: strong savings, plenty of local jobs, family backing.
**Distrust** of employers, not of technology itself, drives his view.
**Boredom**, not fear, is his main worry here.

steps.text: Keep matching supplier invoices by hand in the spreadsheet
Put 200 a month into the savings account
Go to a union branch meeting with my dad

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's another round of cuts dressed up as progress. If software takes over checking and booking, the building society will stop replacing people who leave, and that's what happened to the two older women who did our cheque desk. I'd say it at the union meeting, loudly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job is exactly the kind that shrinks. Matching invoices is checking, and checking is what they said software would take first. I haven't touched any AI tool and I'm not sure I can catch up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd press my manager for a written promise that no one gets cut, and join the union properly. I'd also take the evening course in management accounting my firm offers, because moving up is safer than staying a data-matcher. I'd still avoid the AI tools as long as I could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, and a bit angry. It feels like the ladder is being sawn off just as I step onto it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of your own week would software take over first, and would anyone notice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The invoice matching goes first, no question. Probably nobody would notice for months, because the spreadsheet would just fill itself, and then there'd be one fewer person on our team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask your employer to do, if you could ask for anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for a guarantee in writing, paid training in whatever the new system is, and a say in how it's brought in. Right now we hear about changes after they're done.

say: I'd say this is **cuts** dressed up as progress and call it out at the union.
I'd say fewer older colleagues get replaced, and juniors like me are next.
think: Matching invoices is **checking**, so my own job is the kind that shrinks.
I haven't used AI and I fear I can't **catch up** in time.
do: Ask my manager for a **written promise** and join the union properly.
Start the firm's **management accounting** evening course this winter, aiming to move up.
feel: **Uneasy** and angry, as if the ladder is being sawn off.
S1.quote: Matching invoices is checking, and checking is what they said software would take first. I haven't touched any AI tool and I'm not sure I can catch up.
fieldNote: First scenario where his **refusal** to touch AI becomes a visible weakness.
He turns to the **union** and a course rather than to the tools.

steps.text: Join the union and ask for a written no-cuts promise
Start the management accounting evening course
Cut takeaway meals and put the money in savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a catastrophe and that governments have to step in now: shorter weeks, a basic income, something. If one firm owns the thing that does all the thinking, ordinary people can't be left to the market.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm frightened. Everything I trained for is desk work, and two years is nothing; I'd barely be past my probation. I've no second skill, and I don't use AI, so I couldn't even say I know how to work with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd stop spending on anything extra and go to my dad and the union, because collective action is the only thing that ever got anyone anywhere. I'd also look at the bus depot and the council for steady work. I'd keep the savings in cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, honestly. My stomach drops. I'm twenty-two and I'd have worked for two years in the job I trained for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is short. What do you do in the first month after you hear it's real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first month I'd talk to my dad and his union about what they'd do, and I'd write to my MP, the elected representative for my area. Then I'd budget for six months without income. I'd have a job in a depot or on the buses sorted as a fallback before anything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you say to your family, and what do you leave out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my parents the truth, that I'm scared. I'd leave out how little I understand about what's coming. My mum would worry herself sick if she knew.

say: I'd say governments must step in now with **shorter weeks** or a basic income.
I'd say one firm owning all the thinking can't be left to the market.
think: Desk work is all I trained for and two years is **nothing**, so I'm frightened.
Without a second skill or any AI use, I feel **exposed**.
do: Cut extras, keep savings in **cash**, and budget for six months without pay.
Lean on the **union** and write to my elected representative.
S2.quote: Everything I trained for is desk work, and two years is nothing; I'd barely be past my probation.
fieldNote: **Strongest** scenario for him: no head start in AI and few months in the job.
He looks first to **unions** and politics, then to family.
**Family backing** and savings stop this from being panic.

steps.text: Write to my elected representative demanding shorter weeks
Stop extras and save six months of rent
Ask the bus depot about steady work as a fallback
Talk to my dad and his union about help

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same thing, I'd say it's about who controls it. But with five years, there's time to organise and push for laws, so I'd be at every meeting and march I could find.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years feels survivable, just. I'd have time to build up over twelve thousand in savings and learn at least one thing machines won't take quickly. I still don't want to touch AI, but I may have to learn it the way I'd learn to drive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd finish the management course and take any chance at a role that talks to customers or members. I'd move savings into a fixed account and keep my rent low by staying in the flat share. And I'd help my dad's union write a demand for the building society to retrain staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with some control. Five years gives me a bit of room to breathe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years instead of two. What does that extra time change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years I'd actually try the AI tools, one at a time. I'd hate it, but I'd rather know what it does than just resent it. In two years I wouldn't have had the chance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does your money go during those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Most goes to savings, a little to a course. I'd not buy a flat, because I wouldn't want a mortgage hanging on a job that might not exist. I'd stay in the share and keep the money liquid.

say: I'd say it's about **control**, and five years is time to organise and change the law.
I'd say I'd be at every meeting and march I could find.
think: Five years is **survivable**, so I could build savings and learn one thing machines won't take quickly.
I may have to learn AI the way I'd learn to **drive**.
do: Finish the **management course** and aim for a role that deals with members.
Move savings into a **fixed account** and stay in the flat share.
feel: **Anxious** but with some control and room to breathe.
S3.quote: With five years I'd actually try the AI tools, one at a time. I'd hate it, but I'd rather know what it does than just resent it.
fieldNote: Extra **time** softens his resistance to AI for the first time.
He avoids a **mortgage** to stay flexible.
**Union** work is both a plan and an identity for him.

steps.text: Finish the management accounting course and apply for member-facing roles
Try one AI tool a week on my own invoice data
Move savings into a fixed account and skip buying a flat
Help the union draft a staff retraining demand

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a long time and a lot can be done: unions, new laws, retraining paid by the firms that profit. I'd also say most people won't take it seriously until the final few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years feels almost like nothing happens. I'd be thirty-two. I'd probably still be at the building society or a similar place, maybe running a small team, and I'd think AI will have a go at my job but I'd have time to move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, save steadily, finish the management course and go for a team-lead role in three or four years. I'd learn the AI tools slowly, and be one of the ones who shows others, not the last one in. And I'd stay active in the union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm, a bit uneasy underneath. It's the same end point, just a lot more room to get ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is a long runway. What can you do with that time that you couldn't with two or five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years I could retrain properly, maybe become a financial adviser, where people want a human sitting across from them. I couldn't do that in two years. I'd even think about studying part-time for a professional qualification.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you still want to be in this kind of work by then, or something else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably something with people, not spreadsheets. Maybe advising members on debt or mortgages. I'd want to be the person they trust when they're scared.

say: I'd say ten years is a long time to push for **new laws** and paid retraining.
I'd say most people won't take it seriously until the **last few years**.
think: Ten years feels roomy, and I could even become someone who **teaches** colleagues the tools.
I expect to still be at the society or similar, maybe leading a **small team**.
do: Save steadily, finish the course and aim for a **team-lead** role in 3 to 4 years.
Study part-time for a **professional qualification** in advising people.
S4.quote: With ten years I could retrain properly, maybe become a financial adviser, where people want a human sitting across from them.
fieldNote: **Time** lets him imagine a people-facing future instead of resisting.
Still **reluctant** about AI, but willing to learn slowly.

steps.text: Aim for a team-lead role within four years
Study part-time for an adviser qualification
Learn the AI tools slowly and show others

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, easily. I've just started, I've no second skill and I'm not using any of the new tools. What would help is the union at work, a government that makes firms pay for retraining, and my dad's advice.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: No, I think you got it. Just that I'm not against technology. I'm against it being used on us instead of for us.

headlineQuote: I'm not against technology. I'm against it being used on us instead of for us.
portrait: Gareth is 22, an accounts assistant in a Bristol building society, matching invoices by hand five months into his first job.
He grew up with a bus-driver dad who is a union rep, and he trusts collective action over markets.
He avoids AI tools entirely, which leaves him **calm** if little changes and increasingly worried as change speeds up.
He blames owners and bosses, not technology, and turns to the union, politics and family for protection.
Savings of nine thousand and plenty of nearby jobs keep him from panic, even in the two-year world.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** AGI world worries him most, with no second skill and barely any time in the job.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **union backing**, a government that makes firms pay for retraining, and his dad's advice.
